title: Evaluating Ghost Pipe (Monotropa uniflora) as a Potential Source of Novel Analgesic Compounds
text:
Chronic pain is a complex problem, yet it is one of the most common reasons for seeking medical care. New
treatments are desperately needed to provide safe and effective alternatives to riskier analgesics such as
opioids, and ghost pipe (Monotropa uniflora), a North American medicinal plant that has been used historically
as an anti-inflammatory and analgesic, is a strong candidate for expanding this frontier. This proposal aims to
investigate ghost pipe as a novel source of analgesic compounds by examining its potential pain modulatory
activities and the underlying phytochemicals responsible for this activity.

title: Research Project 1
text: ABSTRACT- PROJECT 1. Disparities in cancer prevention and outcomes by poverty status are rooted in features of the built environment (e.g., walkability, safety, healthcare facilities) and the social environment (e.g., collective efficacy) which have major implications for cancer risk through behaviors such as physical activity and access to preventive care. Adverse neighborhood conditions also exacerbate the stress response, in the form of high allostatic load, which is a risk factor for many cancers. This is a problem in persistent poverty (PP) areas where adverse neighborhood conditions are highly prevalent. However, despite compelling evidence that the living (built and social) environment impacts health-related behaviors and outcomes, including cancer, there are virtually no interventions that determine to what extent modifications of the neighborhood built and social environments reduce cancer risk. The proposed study aims to fill this knowledge gap. We propose a 5-year research project to implement Cancer Prevention through Enhanced EnvironMent (Cancer PREEMpT), to test whether a comprehensive community intervention that improves the neighborhood built and social environments can reduce cancer risk in PP areas. The specific aims of Cancer PREEMpT include: 1) Implementing Cancer PREEMpT and assessing whether the enhancement of living (built and social) environments leads to increased public safety, use of parks and community spaces, community events, and prevention services; 2) Determining the effect of improved living environments on community-level perceptions and behaviors related to cancer risk, such as walkability and safety, self-reported physical activity, social cohesion and collective efficacy, and use of preventive care and cancer screening; and 3) Evaluating the impact of improved living environments on self-reported and objective chronic stress (including allostatic load) and healthcare utilization (including cancer screening). Using a multisectoral approach to bring together citizens, organizations, businesses, and local governments to improve their living environment, the theory-based Cancer PREEMpT intervention will engage community members in five adjacent, urban PP census tracts in Bessemer, Alabama. After a community-engaged needs assessment, modifications will be made in the built and social environments, followed by an evaluation in Year 5. We will apply sequential explanatory mixed methods assessments using a two-group design with independent samples of 300 residents at pre- (Year 1) and post-intervention (Year 5), and focus groups with residents. Finally, to ascertain impact on health care utilization, we will compare Electronic Health Records of all residents of the target area receiving care through the UAB Health System with residents of control urban PP communities similar in racial make-up. Cancer PREEMpT will fill a research gap by providing evidence for reduced cancer risk in PP areas through a community-engaged, stakeholder-supported intervention that improves the living environment.

title: DREAM: Building Equitable Predictive Models for Personalized Diabetes Pharmacotherapy
text: Dr. Kukhareva's application aims to train artificial intelligence (AI) models to predict optimal, personalized type 2 diabetes medication regimens based on individual clinical and demographic factors, ensuring that recommendations are tailored to real-world patient complexities. By analyzing large, national electronic health record (EHR) datasets, this research seeks to improve glycemic control and weight outcomes while evaluating variation in prescribing practices across patient populations. The project aligns with NIH’s mission to improve health outcomes for individuals with type 2 diabetes and to advance data-driven, patient-centered care.

title: Development of potent and safe CRISPR tools for in vivo gene editing using directed evolution
text:
Development of potent and safe CRISPR tools for in vivo gene editing using directed evolution
Research Narrative
Though genome editing technologies provide therapeutic promise many diseases, the CRISPR sgRNA is prone
to cellular instability and immunogenicity thus reducing clinical potential. Full chemical modification has been
essential for the clinical success of past RNA therapeutics, but Cas9 does not function well with fully chemically
modified sgRNA. In this proposal, we describe the development of fully-modified sgRNA:Cas9 pairs to improve
in vivo stability and safety while enabling enhanced genome editing strategies, including self-delivering sgRNA,
multiplexed targets, orthogonal sgRNA:Cas9 pairs, sgRNA redosing, transient editing, and vector inactivation.

title: Mechanisms of ribosome assembly
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health as it addresses a link between defects in eukaryotic
ribosome assembly and resulting human diseases including blood disorders. Ribosomes are the
molecular machines responsible for protein synthesis in all cells. As human diseases associated with
mutations in genes coding for ribosomal proteins or assembly factors are linked to abnormalities in
ribosome synthesis, this research program will be essential to understand the molecular underpinnings
of these diseases.

title: Deciphering The Evolutionary and Biological Impact of Human Admixture
text:
By exchanging genetic variants between populations, admixture has profoundly shaped human
population history, courses of natural selection, and phenotypes and disease burdens across
populations. Failure to consider admixture or the use of wrong models can lead to major adverse
consequences in biomedical applications. This research combines analytical, computational, and
experimental approaches, and will generate novel insight into the evolutionary and functional
consequences of admixture, improve our knowledge of complex traits etiology, and inform strategies
to help reduce health disparity in admixed, underserved populations.

title: Molecular Basis of Human Visual System Disorders
text:
Description
The goal of this research project is to understand the underlying molecular mechanisms of human retinitis
pigmentosa, the most common form of inherited retina diseases. Through studying of the Ddx41 mutant mice
model just established, we plan to reveal how the DDX gene family is involved in retinal degeneration in
human. In parallel, we propose to improve the rate of molecular diagnostic for the disease by identifying novel
pathogenic mutations and disease associated genes that will address a major gap of the field and provide the
basis for developing new therapy.

title: Redox Biology Core
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – GEROSCIENCE REDOX BIOLOGY CORE (GRBC) The goal of the Geroscience Redox Biology (GRB) Core is to provide investigators with a coordinated and comprehensive evaluation of the molecules, pathways, and systems that contribute to oxidative metabolism and oxidative stress using specialized analyses of samples. The state-of-the-art analyses the Core provides allow an integration of measures of redox and energy balance, oxidative damage, and mitochondrial function that are all critical players in aging and age-related diseases and are a key factor in geroscience. The Core leaders, Drs. Van Remmen and Humphries are experts in redox biology and mitochondrial function in aging. The Specific Aims for this Core are the following: Specific Aim 1.) To perform accurate and comprehensive analyses of redox and energetic status, oxidative stress and damage markers and antioxidant protein expression. This includes: GSH/GSSG, and ATP, ADP, and AMP in cells/tissues measured by HPLC; oxidative damage (F2- isoprostanes (lipid peroxidation) and protein carbonyls (protein oxidation) in cells/tissues, and expression of mitochondrial, antioxidant and TCA cycle related proteins in collaboration with the MPAC. Redox and oxidative damage endpoints are present in limited amounts and may be unstable. The expertise in the Core allows for these analyses to be performed with the highest possible rigor, sensitivity and accuracy. In addition, the analyses we provide are especially appropriate for a Core because they require costly equipment and significant technologic expertise that can limit these types of analyses as routine measures in individual laboratories. Finally, because we are analyzing levels of highly specific biological compounds, our redox and oxidative damage assays can be applied to tissues or cells from any living organism. Specific Aim 2.) To perform quantitative high precision measurements of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotides (NADPH/NADP+, NADH/NAD+) and additional markers of redox status by LC/QTOF. NADPH/NADP+ and NADH/NAD+ will be measured in cell/tissue lysates or isolated mitochondria. Additional small molecule markers of redox status and TCA cycle intermediates can be quantified to complement analyses performed in Aim 1. Specific Aim 3.) To provide assays of mitochondrial function using permeabilized tissue, isolated mitochondria, and cell culture models. Mitochondrial function (respiration, ETC activities, oxidant generation) will be measured in isolated mitochondria or fresh tissue using the O2K Oroboros respirometer. Mitochondrial function in cells is measured using the Seahorse Extracellular Flux Analyzer. NADH oxidase, an overall measure of ETC activity and an indicator of mitochondrial function and quantity will be measured spectrophotometrically in frozen tissue. Overall, the Geroscience Redox Biology Core will provide a comprehensive panel of endpoint markers of redox balance and oxidative stress as well as measures of contributing factors such as mitochondrial function and free radical generation that can impact many aspects of aging, healthspan and age-related disease.

title: HPV DNA structure and genome instability at sites of integration
text:
After infection, human papillomavirus (HPV) can integrate into the human genome, sometimes leading to
chromosomal damage and cancer. This project will study how HPV DNA structure promotes genome instability
at integration sites, which may improve detection of high-risk lesions and reveal new targets to prevent cancer
progression.

title: Human Tissue Core
text: Migraine, one of the most common primary headache disorders, affects 1 in 4 US households. This complex neurologic disorder is mediated in part by alterations in trigeminal somatosensation, which manifests as head/fa- cial pain and/or trigeminal allodynia. Effective treatments for migraine are still limited, and our knowledge about human trigeminal system at baseline and migraine conditions are sparse. In response to RFA-NS-22-018, HEAL Initiative: Discovery and Functional Evaluation of Human Pain-associated Genes & Cells, we propose to form the Penn Human Precision Pain Center (Penn HPPC) to elucidate molecular, cellular, epigenetic, and physiological profiles of human trigeminal ganglion (TG) sensory neurons at baseline and migraine conditions. The Penn HPPC will be composed of Penn and international investigators with multidisciplinary expertise. The PI, two MPIs, and two co-Is are currently collaborating on a single-soma deep RNA-seq of human dorsal root ganglion (DRG) project, which form a strong foundation for this application. The Penn HPPC will contain three cores and perform three projects. Among them, the human tissue core will function as the sole entity for procuring and storing human tissues and distributing human tissues among research projects. The Penn HPPC human tissue procurement and processing core will also coordinate with other U19 centers and the NIH HEAL Initiative PRECISION Human Pain network for human tissue procurement, sharing, and SOP (Standard Operat- ing Procedure) development. The human tissue core will be led by the PI, Dr. Luo, and supported by her research associate, Dr. Yu, and a coordinator. The human tissue core will also include two UPenn neurosurgeons, Drs Ali Zarina and Eric Zager, and a coordinator in the department of neurosurgery. Specifically, the human tissue core will coordinate with different human tissue procurement sites, including the human tissue cores of other U19 centers, for procuring human trigeminal ganglion (TGs) and dorsal root ganglion (DRG) tissues, perform quality control of all procured tissues, stock and archive the tissues, distribute tissues among the three research pro- jects, ensure compliances and trainings related to human tissues, and work with the administrative core to dis- seminate optimized protocols and procedures related to human TGs and DRGs to the HEAL community and the pain research field. Together with other components of the Penn HPPC, the human tissue procurement and processing core will help to achieve the proposed goals of Penn HPPC as well as the overarching goal of the NIH HEAL Initiative PRECISION Human Pain network.

title: Delineate the Role of GSTP1 in Advanced Prostate Cancer
text:
The major goal of the proposed project is to test the role of GSTP1 in aggressive prostate cancer. The study will
also define novel mechanisms through which GSTP1 contributes to the development of the advanced disease.
Completion of the proposed research will give us insights into new mechanisms underlying the development of
aggressive prostate cancer and open novel avenues for therapeutic interventions.

title: Tumor-barcoding coupled with high-throughput sequencing for quantitative radiogenomics of the abscopal response in NSCLC
text:
The work we have proposed has a direct impact on the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer with
chemoradiation and immunotherapy. As resistance mechanisms of chemoradiation with immunotherapy are not
being intensely studied using relevant preclinical cancer models, our findings can have an immediate and large
impact on the field. Lastly, the study of resistance mechanisms against chemoradiation with immunotherapy in
lung cancer may allow a broader understanding of resistance mechanisms in other cancers and expose new
pathways to target treatment resistance.

title: Evaluation of Post-Acute Care Access and Outcomes: Influence of Social Determinants of Health on Urban and Rural Rehabilitation Service Areas Before and After COVID-19
text:
The study is essential for understanding the influence of social determinants of health (SDH) on post-acute
care (PAC) rehabilitation access and variation in quality-of-care outcomes across the nation. This project will
evaluate SDH variables and their association with PAC access across PAC settings, across rural and urban
rehabilitation service areas, and how these associations are moderated by racial and ethnic population density
and the COVID pandemic as well as how these factors impact readmission and successful community
discharge outcomes. The study informs clinicians, researchers, communities, policy debates, and can lead to
better PAC outcomes, and allow us to better understand SDH factors that affect quality-of-care.

title: Integrated Dual-frequency Ultrasound Catheter for Accelerated Sonothrombolysis (iDUCAS)
text:
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) affects two million Americans every year and can cause pulmonary
embolism (PE), which is fatal in ~10% of acute cases, with higher rates in patients with cancer. Current DVT
treatment techniques include systemic administration of thrombolytic drugs and endovascular catheter-based
thrombectomy, which is either slow and/or carries risk of vessel damage. Our renewal proposal will develop an
integrated dual-frequency catheter-accelerated sonothrombolysis system (iDUCAS), which can quickly and
safely treat even the most advanced and heterogeneous clots and reduce the occurrence of complications,
morbidity, and mortality of DVT.

title: Structure-based in-silico prediction of peptide interactions.
text:
Automated docking is a workhorse for rational drug design, however, applying these methods to peptides has remained
challenging, thus impeding the rational designing of peptide-based therapeutic approaches.
We have been at the forefront of the development peptide-docking docking methods with our state-of-the-art physics-
based docking engine, AutoDock CrankPep (ADCP), which can successfully dock linear and cyclic peptides with up to
20 standard amino acids, and we have established that AlphaFold2 multimer and ADCP can be combined to achieve
higher docking success rates.
We will further develop ADCP to support more therapeutic peptides; synergistically combine it with AlphaFold2
multimer; and explore the use of these protein-peptide docking methods for approaching peptide-peptide docking,
yielding docking tools that will impact the research of many computational and medicinal chemists and biologist,
contribute to our understanding of biological processes, and significantly advance biomedical research.

title: Proteomic interrogation of N-terminal acetylation on misfolded proteins in extracellular vesicles
text:
Protein misfolding, often accompanied by abnormal post-translational modifications, plays a critical role in
neurodegenerative diseases, notably Alzheimer’s disease (AD). We propose in this project to discover and
investigate the important molecular connections among protein misfolding, covalent modifications, and
clearance for future AD diagnosis and monitoring.

title: Enhanced detection of anomaly in bone age X-ray for diagnosis of childhood growth disorder
text:
Children often present with suboptimal linear growth, yet identifying the underlying genetic etiology remains
challenging. Although the left-hand bone age X-ray is a routine screening tool for growth concerns, its potential
to uncover anomalies linked to genetic disorders has not been fully realized. By systematically examining these
radiographic findings, we aim to enhance insights for informed and precise diagnosis in clinical settings and drive
the discovery of novel genetic causes of childhood growth disorders.

title: Targeting early events in oral chronic graft-versus-host disease to improve oralhealth in transplant patients
text:
Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation is an effective treatment for patients with certain cancers, blood
disorders and primary immunodeficiencies, however, an estimated 2000 Americans annually develop chronic Graft-
Versus-Host-Disease (cGVHD) in the mouth after transplant. This immune condition is difficult to treat, and this
research will deepen understanding of the initial causes of cGVHD in the mouth. Our findings will have broad
implications for transplant immunology and for understanding how the immune system functions in
autoinflammatory oral disease.

title: Community-academic partnership to address environmental contamination and health
text:
Residents of northern Lake County, Indiana, have expressed great concern regarding the potential health
impacts resulting from ongoing release of environmental pollutants from the area’s numerous metal, petroleum,
and chemical industries. There is substantial scientific data that exposure to individual metals and volatile
organic compounds can result in neurotoxicity and other health outcomes; however, there is very little information
regarding the cumulative impact of exposure to a complex mixture of these compounds. This community-
engaged research project will address both knowledge gaps by characterizing resident exposure to multiple
environmental chemicals, determining the association of exposure to these mixtures with self-reported health
outcomes and neurological function.
